# Sādhinajātaka (Ja 494)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sādhinajātaka* (Ja 494) is a canonical narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection. According to the framing story (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha related it while residing at Jetavana to lay disciples observing the fast-day (*uposatha*) vows, explaining that wise men of antiquity ascended bodily to heaven by virtue of keeping these precepts [Fausböll 1887]. In the tale of the past, the Bodhisatta was Sādhina, the righteous king of Mithilā, whose exemplary charity and virtue prompted Sakka to invite him bodily to Tāvatiṃsa heaven [Fausböll 1887; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. When the devas offered King Sādhina a share of their own celestial merit so he could remain with them, he declined the gift and chose to return to the human realm to cultivate his own merit and spiritual development [Appleton; Fausböll 1887]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that Sakka was Anuruddha, King Nārada was Ānanda, and King Sādhina was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1887].

King Sādhina is traditionally celebrated alongside Mandhātā, Nimi, and Guttila as one of four beings who ascended to Indra's heaven in their human bodies [Wiltshire 1990; Rhys Davids 1890]. In modern scholarship, the *Sādhinajātaka* is frequently examined—notably following analyses by James P. McDermott—as early canonical evidence of ambivalence toward the practice of merit transference: by having the Bodhisatta decline the devas' offered merit to generate his own kamma, the text affirms personal responsibility over dependence on external merit [Appleton; De Rauw 2008; Fenn 1994; Doniger O'Flaherty 1980].

 DharmaNexus confirms substantial Pali-internal text reuse with the *Nimijātaka* (Ja 541, matching §10.2–13.6 of this text with §167.4–170.6) and with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, while also automatically aligning passages with Tibetan texts including the *Pitāputrasamāgamana* (D0060), *Saddharmānusmṛtyupasthāna* (D0287-2), *Lalitavistara* (D0095), and the *Jātakamālā* (D4150) [DharmaNexus].
